observation: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) found time-matched retrieval practice produced 61% recall at one week versus 40% for time-matched rereading — one of the few learning-technique comparisons that actually equates study time between conditions.
claim: Retrieval practice decisively beats rereading at equal study time, a rare case where 'gain per minute' is directly measurable rather than inferred.
mechanism: Effortful retrieval (generating an answer from memory) produces more durable encoding than passive re-exposure to the same content in the same amount of time.

implications.text: Prefer retrieval-check interactions over passive re-reading whenever a time-equated comparison is possible; this is the strongest literature-backed lever for gain-per-minute.

observation: Schroeder, Nesbit, Anguiano & Adesope (2018, meta-analysis, 142 effect sizes, n=11,814) found constructing a concept map (g=0.72) produces a substantially larger benefit than studying a pre-made one (g=0.43), against an overall concept-map effect of g=0.58.
claim: If Riemann ever offers a 'build your own L2 map' mode (dragging/renaming/connecting section nodes), it should produce roughly a 0.3-g benefit over just reading the auto-generated tree, making lightly-editable tree nodes a quantified, not just plausible, feature.
mechanism: Actively constructing relational structure recruits deeper processing than passively studying an already-built structure.
context: meta-analysis; full text paywalled, top-line numbers read via search aggregation

implications.text: If tree-editing is ever built, treat it as an opt-in, evidenced learning-boosting feature (not just a convenience), since construction produces a real g=0.29 advantage over passive study.

observation: RSVP/Spritz-style flashing-word reading reliably degrades literal comprehension above roughly 250-350 wpm, with genuinely conflicting findings across studies on whether inferential comprehension is spared or also degrades; a small qualitative study (n=9 undergrads) found RSVP acceptable for skimming but explicitly not suitable for real academic study needs.
claim: An RSVP mode should not be shipped as a general reading substitute; if built, it should be scoped tightly to L0 (one-line gist) and literal-fact skimming, never comprehension-critical or inference-heavy material.
mechanism: Loss of regressions (re-fixations that normal reading uses for comprehension repair) is the likely mechanistic reason RSVP degrades comprehension, independent of the unresolved inferential-comprehension question.
population: general adult readers; small undergraduate sample (n=9) for the real-study-use finding
context: mixed lab comprehension studies and one small real-task qualitative study

implications.text: Restrict any RSVP mode to L0/literal-fact skimming use only, and say so explicitly in the UI rather than presenting it as a general reading substitute.

observation: Kalyuga's rapid verification method (present partial/plausible solution steps, ask the learner to rapidly judge correct/incorrect) diagnoses prior-knowledge level in roughly 1/3.8 the time of full problem-solving while correlating r=.66 with full test scores, validated in well-structured procedural/STEM domains.
claim: A fast true/false rapid-verification probe (2-3 plausible one-line claims from the material, mark right/wrong) is a cheap, evidenced way to diagnose prior knowledge and gate how much scaffolding Riemann shows, though it's untested for open-ended reading material specifically.
mechanism: Rapid plausibility judgments on partial steps correlate well with full-test performance while taking a fraction of the time, because they tap the same underlying knowledge structure without requiring full problem execution.
population: general students in well-structured STEM/procedural domains (algebra, electrical troubleshooting)
context: multiple validation studies by the same research group over ~15 years

implications.text: Show 2-3 plausible-sounding one-line claims (some true, some subtly wrong) before expanding a document, as a cheap diagnostic that gates scaffolding level — a genuinely new instantiation for open-ended reading, not a directly transferred one.

observation: Khan Academy discontinued its spatial/graph-like 'Knowledge Map' (a starry-night visualization) in 2013 in favor of a simpler five-tier ordinal mastery ladder (Not started/Attempted/Familiar/Proficient/Mastered); Duolingo's Birdbrain similarly surfaces a coarse skill-tree map rather than exposing its internal proficiency estimate as a number.
claim: 'What Sam knows' should default to a surfaced ordinal per-topic ladder rather than a rich graph/map overlay, even if the underlying model is richer — a graph-shaped 'map of my competence' has a real, shipped failure case at scale.
mechanism: A retired real-world product data point shows a graph-shaped learner-competence overlay did not survive contact with actual daily consumer use, distinct from the separately-supported case for the abstraction tree itself being graph-shaped.
population: general consumer ed-tech users (product history, not a controlled study)

implications.text: Surface 'what Sam knows across documents' as an ordinal per-topic ladder (not-started/familiar/proficient), reserving any richer graph model for the abstraction tree's own internal structure, not a competence overlay.

observation: Li, Dey & Forlizzi's (2010) stage-based model of personal-informatics systems (preparation → collection → integration → reflection → action) finds barriers cascade forward: a failure at collection guarantees failure at reflection and action.
claim: Riemann's longitudinal 'what Sam knows' system must build reliable, low-friction collection (which documents opened, to what level, for how long) before investing in integration or reflection, since a broken collection stage makes everything downstream unreliable regardless of sophistication.
mechanism: Personal-informatics barriers cascade: later stages cannot compensate for missing or unreliable data captured at the collection stage.
population: general (Quantified Self community interviews, qualitative HCI framework)

implications.text: Sequence longitudinal-modeling work: build reliable collection (already near-free from the zoom-dial's own interaction logs) before integration or reflection features.

observation: Outside retrieval practice vs. rereading, the technique literature (self-explanation, elaborative interrogation, summarization, concept mapping) reports effectiveness, not effectiveness-per-minute-spent; the one located time-on-task data point (elaborative learning 32 min vs. plain reading 28 min) is a single, weakly-sourced figure, not a systematic literature.
claim: Riemann cannot import a 'minutes per technique' budget from the literature for most techniques; it must calibrate its own budget-allocation model empirically from usage logs (dwell time × outcome signal).
mechanism: Almost no study in this literature equates or reports study time across conditions, so 'gain per minute' is largely unmeasured outside the retrieval-practice comparison.
population: general (absence-of-evidence observation across the technique-efficacy literature)
context: literature gap, not a positive finding

implications.text: Treat any literature-derived 'minutes per technique' estimate as a rough prior to be overwritten quickly by Riemann's own logged time-to-outcome data.
